facts.claim: The Carrington Event was the most intense geomagnetic storm in recorded history, peaking on 1–2 September 1859 during solar cycle 10.
It created strong auroral displays that were reported globally and caused sparking and even fires in telegraph stations.
Telegraph systems all over Europe and North America failed, in some cases giving their operators electric shocks.
On 23 July 2012, a Carrington-class solar superstorm was observed, but its trajectory narrowly missed Earth by a margin of roughly nine days.
In June 2013, researchers at Lloyd's of London and AER estimated the cost of a similar event in the present to the US alone at US$600 billion to $2.6 trillion.

narration.text: Why a repeat of 1859 could cost $2.6 trillion.
The 1859 Carrington storm set telegraph stations on fire.
Telegraph systems across Europe and North America failed.
Some operators even got electric shocks.
In 2012, a similar storm missed Earth by about 9 days.
A 2013 estimate put a repeat's U.S. cost at $600 billion to $2.6 trillion.
Today, long power lines and satellites would take the hit.
So the same storm would cost far more now than then.

narration.text: Why auroras glow about 100 kilometres above you.
None have been found below 70 kilometres.
Solar particles excite oxygen atoms high in the air.
Lower down, oxygen glows green at 557.7 nanometres.
Higher up, it glows red at 630 nanometres.
Airliners cruise far below, around 10 kilometres up.
So the northern lights happen at the edge of space.

So each eclipse touches just a thin strip of the planet.
Totality lasts minutes; the longest calculated reaches 7 minutes 29 seconds.
That's why eclipse chasers travel to the path.
So total eclipses are common for Earth, and rare for you.

In 1978, Kessler found that 42 percent of cataloged debris was the result of 19 events, primarily explosions of spent rocket stages.
Optical telescopes and short-wavelength radar measurements demonstrated that the published population count was at least 50% too low.
The list could not easily account for objects under 20 cm (8 in) in size.

narration.text: Why one crash in orbit could close space.
Scientists call this cascade the Kessler syndrome.
Kessler proposed it in 1978.
Then, 42% of tracked debris came from just 19 events.
Radar later showed debris counts were at least 50% too low.
Objects under 20 centimetres were hard to track at all.
A runaway cascade could make some orbits unusable for years.
So the biggest threat to satellites may be other satellites.

Halley concluded that all three comets were the same object returning about every 76 years, a period that has since been found to vary between 72 and 80 years.

Planets' gravity tugs it, shifting each return.
In 1986, probes flew within 8,030 kilometres of it.
So for most people, it's a once-in-a-lifetime sight.

facts.claim: One solar day (sunrise to sunrise) on Mercury lasts for around 176 Earth days, or twice Mercury's sidereal year.

At perihelion, the equatorial subsolar point climbs to a temperature of about 700 K.

narration.text: Why one Mercury day lasts 176 Earth days.
That's twice as long as its 88-day year.
It spins slowly, locked in a 3:2 dance with its orbit.
At noon, the surface can reach about 700 kelvin.
The night side averages −163 °C.
Polar craters never see sunlight at all.
With no atmosphere, nothing evens the heat out.
So the closest planet to the Sun still has frozen corners.

Some pieces were up to 2 kilometres wide.
One fireball plume rose over 3,000 kilometres.
The impacts ran from July 16 to 22.
Each hit left dark scars visible from Earth.
So Jupiter works as a shredder, not just a shield.

So the scariest star in Orion is mostly a spectacle.

facts.claim: It has a marked axial tilt of 82.23°, with a retrograde rotation period of 17 hours and 14 minutes.
In an 84-Earth-year orbital period around the Sun, its poles get around 42 years of continuous sunlight, followed by 42 years of continuous darkness.
The planet's atmosphere has the lowest minimum temperature (49 K (−224 °C)) of all of the Solar System's planets.
As of 2026, it has been visited only once when in 1986 the Voyager 2 probe flew by the planet.

narration.text: Why Uranus's poles get 42 years of sunlight.
Then they get 42 years of darkness.
Its axis is tilted 82.23 degrees, nearly on its side.
One orbit takes 84 Earth years.
Tilt Earth like that, and each pole gets decades-long days.
Seasons would swing between endless glare and endless night.
Only Voyager 2 has visited Uranus, in 1986.
So Earth's gentle seasons come from a modest tilt.

Standing in those winds, nothing on Earth could hold you.
So the coldest planets can have the wildest weather.

Then soot and dust would dim sunlight for years.
The real killer wasn't the crater. It was the sky.

So the nearest new world is close, and still a mystery.

New Horizons was the first spacecraft to visit Pluto and its moons, making a flyby on July 14, 2015.
Pluto has a moderately eccentric and inclined orbit, ranging from 30 to 49 astronomical units from the Sun.

narration.text: Why Pluto lost its planet status in 2006.
The discovery of Eris in 2005 forced the question.
Eris is more massive than Pluto.
Planets must clear their orbits, and Pluto shares the Kuiper belt.
Keep Pluto a planet, and many Kuiper worlds would join it.
Sunlight takes 5.5 hours to reach it.
New Horizons flew past it in 2015.
So Pluto didn't shrink. Our definition grew up.

facts.claim: Over the last two centuries the dipole strength has been decreasing at a rate of about 6.3% per century.
Measurements since Gauss in 1832 show a relative decay of about 10% over the last 150 years.
There have been at least 183 reversals over the last 83 million years, on average once every ~450,000 years.
The latest, the Brunhes–Matuyama reversal, occurred 780,000 years ago.
Some sources estimate the four most recent reversals took on average 7,000 years.

narration.text: Earth's magnetic field is already weakening.
Its main dipole has faded about 6.3% per century.
Fields have flipped 183 times in 83 million years.
The last flip was 780,000 years ago.
Now switch it off completely, for just one day.
Satellites and power grids would take more charged particles.
But the air wouldn't vanish in a day; that takes far longer.
So we'd survive, but our technology would feel it first.

Between 1816 and 1819, major typhus epidemics occurred in parts of Europe, including Ireland, Italy, Switzerland, and Scotland, precipitated by the famine.
The ice dam collapsed catastrophically in June 1818, killing forty people in the resulting flood.

Global temperatures dropped by 0.4 to 0.7 °C.
That small shift was enough to ruin harvests.
Famine helped trigger typhus epidemics across Europe until 1819.
Today, a similar eruption would hit global grain markets at once.
Food trade would spread the shortage, and the price shock, worldwide.
So a single volcano could still test the world's food supply.

facts.claim: This massive desiccation left a deep dry basin, reaching 3 to 5 km (1.9 to 3.1 mi) deep below normal sea level, with a few hypersaline pockets.
When that was shut off sometime between 6.5 to 6 MYBP, net evaporative loss set in at the rate of around 3,300 cubic kilometres yearly.
The Messinian salinity crisis ended with the Strait of Gibraltar finally reopening 5.33 Ma, when the Atlantic rapidly filled up the Mediterranean basin in what is known as the Zanclean flood.
The Sorbas Basin was filled with evaporites at 5.5 million years ago (Ma), compared to the main basin at 5.96 Ma.
Research has suggested that the desiccation-flooding cycle may have repeated several times during the last 630,000 years of the Miocene epoch.

narration.text: Why the Mediterranean once lost 3,300 km³ a year.
It left a basin up to 5 kilometres deep.
Cut off from the Atlantic, evaporation outpaced every river.
Salt piled up in thick layers across the seabed.
The drying and flooding may have repeated several times.
It ended 5.33 million years ago, when Gibraltar reopened.
The Atlantic poured back in, in the Zanclean flood.
So one narrow strait decides whether a sea exists.

facts.claim: Earth currently has an axial tilt of about 23.44°.
Mars's obliquity is quite variable over millions of years; it varies as much as 0° to 60° depending on perturbations of the planets.
Nutation adds short-period oscillations of about 9.2 arcseconds over about 18.6 years.

narration.text: Double Earth's tilt, and seasons turn extreme.

Double it, and months of polar night creep toward mid-latitudes.
Summers would get hotter, winters darker and longer.
Mars shows how wild it gets: its tilt swings between 0 and 60 degrees.
Earth's own tilt barely wobbles today, only by arcseconds.
So a stable tilt is one reason seasons are survivable.

facts.claim: On 21 August 1986, a limnic eruption at Lake Nyos in northwestern Cameroon killed 1,746 people and 3,500 livestock.
The eruption triggered the sudden release of about 100,000–300,000 tons of carbon dioxide (CO2).
The supersaturated deep water rapidly mixed with the upper layers of the lake, where the reduced pressure allowed the stored CO2 to effervesce out of solution.
Since carbon dioxide is 50% more dense than air, the cloud hugged the ground and moved down the valleys, where there were various villages.
A degassing system has since been installed at the lake, with the aim of reducing the concentration of CO2 in the waters.

narration.text: A lake once exploded and killed 1,746 people.
It didn't burst with water. It burst with CO2.
Lake Nyos released 100,000 to 300,000 tons of carbon dioxide.
Its deep water was supersaturated, like a shaken soda.
Once mixed upward, the gas fizzed out of solution.
CO2 is 50% denser than air, so the cloud hugged valleys.
Villagers below had no warning and nothing to breathe.
Pipes now vent the gas slowly to prevent a repeat.

Ice covered about 25% of the land.
The peak came between 25,200 and 23,100 years ago.
Bring it back, and today's ports would sit far inland.
Land bridges would reappear between continents.
So coastlines are just where the ice happens to leave the sea.

facts.claim: The snowball Earth hypothesis postulates that the planet's surface froze more than 650 Ma.
According to modelling, an ice–albedo feedback would result in glacial ice rapidly advancing to the equator once the glaciers spread to within 25° to 30° of the equator.
Palaeomagnetic measurements have indicated that some sediments of glacial origin were deposited within 10 degrees of the equator, although the accuracy of this reconstruction is in question.
A record from Oman covers the period from 712 to 545 million years ago, a time span containing the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations.

narration.text: Earth may have frozen to the equator before.
Scientists call it Snowball Earth, over 650 million years ago.
Ice reflects sunlight, which cools the planet further.
Models show ice runs away once it reaches 25 to 30 degrees of the equator.
Some glacial rocks may have formed within 10 degrees of the equator.
Escaping it would need volcanic CO2 to build up for ages.
Life survived anyway, in pockets we still debate.
So Earth's climate has a freezing tipping point, not just a warming one.

facts.claim: In 1960, the Aral Sea had been the world's fourth-largest lake with an area of 68,000 km2 (26,000 sq mi) and a volume of 1,100 km3.
In 2004, the sea's surface area was 17,160 km2 (6,630 sq mi), 25% of its original size, and a nearly fivefold increase in salinity had killed most of its flora and fauna.
Large scale construction of irrigation canals first began in the 1930s and was greatly increased in the 1960s.
The North Aral Sea's surface increased from 2,550 square kilometers in 2003 to 3,300 square kilometers in 2008.
By 1988, Uzbekistan was the world's largest exporter of cotton.

narration.text: Why a sea shrank to 25% without a drought.
It was the world's fourth-largest lake in 1960.
It covered 68,000 square kilometres.
Soviet irrigation diverted its rivers to grow cotton.
By 2004, it was down to 17,160 square kilometres.
Salinity rose nearly fivefold, killing most fish and plants.
A dam has since let the North Aral partly recover.
So a sea can vanish without a drought, just by thirst upstream.

The storm finally dissipated over three hours after touching down.

narration.text: Why one tornado stayed on the ground three hours.

It raced forward at about 100 kilometres per hour.
Debris landed nearly 80 kilometres away.
In Murphysboro alone, 234 people died.
In total, 695 people were killed.
There was no tornado warning system back then.
So warnings matter most when storms move this fast.

Losing it wouldn't suffocate us, but it would release huge carbon stores.
It would also erase species found nowhere else.
So the Amazon's real value is carbon and life, not air.

topics.misconception: The famous 1913 record is disputed; the reliable high is 54.4 °C.
editorialTitles: What a Summer in Death Valley Does to You
Why Death Valley's Nights Are the Real Danger

facts.claim: The highest reliable temperature in Death Valley is 130 °F (54.4 °C) recorded at Furnace Creek on August 16, 2020 and July 9, 2021.
Some modern meteorologists now dispute the accuracy of the 1913 temperature measurement due to regional mismatch and observer issues.
Summer nights provide little relief: overnight lows may dip just into the 82 to 98 °F (28 to 37 °C) range.
The greatest number of consecutive days with a maximum temperature of at least 100 °F (38 °C) was 154, in the summer of 2001.

narration.text: Death Valley hit 54.4 °C in 2020.
It's the highest reliable temperature recorded there.
The famous 1913 record is now disputed.
Summer nights often stay between 28 and 37 °C.
In 2001, it logged 154 straight days of at least 38 °C.
Without shade and water, heat stroke comes quickly.
Your body cools by sweating, and dry air speeds it up.
So the danger isn't one hot afternoon. It's heat that never breaks.

facts.claim: It is estimated that the lake contains around 19% of the unfrozen fresh water on the planet.
It is also the world's oldest lake at 25–30 million years, and among the clearest.
In geological terms, the rift is young and active; it widens about 4 mm (0.16 in) per year.
The lake is divided into three basins: North, Central, and South, with depths about 900 m, 1,600 m, and 1,400 m, respectively.
In the deepest parts of the lake, from about 300 m, the temperature is stable at 3.1–3.4 °C with only minor annual variations.

narration.text: One lake holds 19% of unfrozen fresh water.
Lake Baikal, in Siberia, is also the world's oldest.
It formed 25 to 30 million years ago.
Its rift still widens about 4 millimetres a year.
Its basins reach 900, 1,600 and 1,400 metres deep.
Below 300 metres, it stays at 3.1 to 3.4 °C year-round.
Drain it, and a fifth of Earth's unfrozen fresh water disappears.
So one Siberian rift holds a startling share of our fresh water.

topics.misconception: A shutdown wouldn't plunge Europe into an ice age; a 15–20 °C crash is considered incorrect.
editorialTitles: What If the Atlantic Current Shut Down
Why an AMOC Collapse Isn't an Ice Age

facts.claim: The AMOC carries up to 25% of the total heat toward the northern hemisphere, and plays an important role in the climate around northwest Europe.
There is a consensus the AMOC keeps northern and western Europe warmer than it would be otherwise, with the difference of 4 °C (7.2 °F) and 10 °C (18 °F) depending on the area.
Climate models predict the AMOC will further weaken during the 21st century.
A cooling of up to 15–20 °C (27–36 °F) is generally considered incorrect.
D-O events are best known for the rapid warming of between 8 °C (15 °F) and 15 °C (27 °F) that occurred in Greenland over several decades.

narration.text: Up to 25% of northern heat rides one current.
Climate models say it will weaken this century.
It keeps parts of Europe 4 to 10 °C warmer.
Claims of a 15 to 20 °C crash are considered incorrect.
But winters would harden, and rain belts would shift south.
In Greenland's past, similar swings brought 8 to 15 °C within decades.
So the danger isn't an ice age. It's speed.

narration.text: One earthquake ruptured 1,300 kilometres of seafloor.
The shaking lasted at least ten minutes.
Its magnitude is estimated at 9.1 to 9.3.
Waves reached up to 30 metres high.
In total, 227,898 people died across the Indian Ocean.
Seismic waves crossed the planet in about 22 minutes.
The Indian Ocean had no tsunami warning system then.
So the deadliest part of a tsunami is the time without warning.

facts.claim: In keeping with the supercontinent cycle, Pangaea Proxima could form within the next 250 million years.
About 125 million years from now, the Atlantic Ocean is predicted to stop widening and to begin to shrink, as seafloor spreading gives way to subduction.
Rifts will form, and Pangaea Proxima will split up once more in 400 to 500 million years.
Research published in 2022 supports an Amasia scenario within 200 to 300 million years.

narration.text: Why the Atlantic may vanish in 250 million years.
The continents could fuse into Pangaea Proxima.
In about 125 million years, the Atlantic stops widening.
Its seafloor would then start sinking back into Earth.
Another study favours a merger across the Pacific, within 200 to 300 million years.
Either way, it could split again after 400 to 500 million years.
Its interior would sit thousands of kilometres from any ocean.
So the map you know is one frame in a slow cycle.

facts.claim: The system erupted violently over an eight-month period between June 1783 and February 1784 from the Laki fissure and the adjoining volcano Grímsvötn.
About 80% of sheep (190,500 head), 50% of cattle (11,500 head), and 50% of horses (28,000 head) died because of dental and skeletal fluorosis from the 8 million tons of fluorine that were released.
An estimated 20% of the population died in the famine after the fissure eruptions ensued, with about 8,000 excess deaths.
The gases were carried by the convective eruption column to altitudes around 15 km (50,000 ft).

narration.text: Why one eruption killed 80% of Iceland's sheep.
Laki released about 8 million tons of fluorine.
It erupted for eight months, from June 1783.
Fluorine poisoned the grass that livestock ate.
Half of all cattle and horses died too.
Famine followed, killing about 20% of the population.
Its gases rose about 15 kilometres high.
So a volcano's deadliest weapon can be invisible.

facts.claim: Near Earth's surface, the acceleration due to gravity is 9.8 m/s2.
Gravity on Earth's surface varies by around 0.7%, from 9.7639 m/s2 on Nevado Huascarán to 9.8337 m/s2 at the Arctic Ocean surface.
The conventional value for standard gravity is 9.80665 m/s2, originally adopted by the CGPM in 1901.
The weight of an object on Earth's surface is the downward force on it, force equals mass times acceleration.

narration.text: Gravity doubles tomorrow. Your weight doubles too.
Your mass stays the same. Only the pull changes.
Weight is mass times gravity's pull, 9.8 metres per second squared.
Double it, and every step lifts twice the load.
Today, gravity varies across Earth by only about 0.7%.
So a doubling dwarfs every difference you've ever felt.
Your heart would push blood uphill against twice the pull.
So the first strain lands on bodies, not buildings.

Why Absolute Zero Can Never Be Reached

facts.claim: The Kelvin scale is defined so that absolute zero is 0 K, equivalent to −273.15 °C on the Celsius scale, and −459.67 °F on the Fahrenheit scale.
The current world record for effective temperatures was set in 2021 at 38 picokelvin through matter-wave lensing of rubidium Bose–Einstein condensates.
In 2018, scientists at the University of Bremen achieved temperatures as low as 38 picokelvin (pK), 38 trillionths of a degree above absolute zero.
0 kelvins is defined as the point at which pressure or volume would vanish in an ideal gas.
By 1845, Michael Faraday had reached a new record for lowest temperatures by reaching −130 °C (−202 °F; 143 K).

narration.text: Nothing has ever reached −273.15 °C: absolute zero.
The record is 38 trillionths of a degree above.
It's where an ideal gas's pressure would fall to zero.
Physics lets you approach it, but never arrive.
Even there, particles would keep a minimum jiggle, called zero-point motion.
Near it, helium flows without friction and climbs container walls.
So absolute zero isn't stillness. It's a limit you chase forever.

The fine-structure constant is approximately 0.0072973525643, about 1/137.

narration.text: Double light speed, and atoms change.
It's not just faster internet. Chemistry itself shifts.
Light is fixed at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second.
A number called the fine-structure constant is about 1/137.
It shrinks when light gets faster, and it governs how atoms bond.
Double light speed, and it halves.
Some theories say life needs it between 1/180 and 1/85.
Halved, it falls outside that window, so the answer is chemistry, not speed.

facts.claim: By taking into account the realistic density distribution inside the Earth, the expected fall-through time is reduced from 42 to 38 minutes.
The straight line path between London and Paris would only require a maximum depth of 2.4 kilometres.
Such a tunnel would have an initial declination of 1.57 degrees.
The same idea was proposed, without calculation, by Lewis Carroll in 1893 in Sylvie and Bruno Concluded.

narration.text: Fall through Earth, and you'd arrive in 38 minutes.
Gravity pulls you down, then slows you back up.
For a uniform planet, the trip takes 42 minutes.
Earth's dense core speeds you up, cutting it to 38.
Even London to Paris would need only a 2.4-kilometre-deep tunnel.
Without air and friction, you'd pop out at the far side.
With them, you'd oscillate, then settle at the centre.
So gravity alone could run a train, if friction didn't exist.

Atomic clocks even detect gravity's version across 33 centimetres.
Near light speed, one year aboard could equal many years at home.
So speed doesn't just move you. It moves you through time.

narration.text: Why Earth's spin can't steer your toilet.
Identical toilets drain the same way in both hemispheres.
The bowl's shape sets the swirl, not Earth's spin.
The Coriolis effect is real, but tiny at sink scale.
In one careful test, a still tank took 20 minutes to drain.
Only after about 15 minutes did Earth's rotation show.
At hurricane scale, though, it sets the direction of the spin.
So Earth's rotation steers storms, not your bathroom.

Lene Hau's team did it in 1998 using ultracold atoms.

In 2004, a semiconductor slowed light to 9.6 kilometres per second.
The light isn't tired. It's delayed by how it interacts with matter.
Slow light could one day help store signals in optical chips.
So light's famous speed limit is only its top speed.

topics.misconception: Space battles aren't loud; sound can't cross a vacuum.
editorialTitles: Why Space Is Silent
How Fast Sound Travels Through Everything

facts.claim: At 0 °C (32 °F), the speed of sound in dry air (sea level 14.7 psi) is about 331 m/s (1,086 ft/s; 1,192 km/h; 740 mph; 643 kn).
In 1826, Colladon and Sturm found a value of 1437.8 m/s in water at 8 C.
For a typical steel alloy, K = 170 GPa, G = 80 GPa and p = 7700 kg/m3, yielding a compressional speed of 6,000 m/s.
In an exceptionally stiff material such as diamond, sound travels at 12,000 m/s (39,000 ft/s), about 35 times its speed in air.

narration.text: Why explosions in space make no sound.
Sound needs matter, and space has almost none.
In air at 0 °C, sound moves about 331 metres per second.
In water, it's about 1,438 metres per second.
In steel, around 6,000.
In diamond, up to 12,000 metres per second.
Stiffer materials carry sound faster.
So space isn't loud. It's the quietest place there is.

editorialTitles: Why Earth's Core Is as Hot as the Sun
The Solid Ball of Fire Beneath Your Feet

facts.claim: It is primarily a solid ball with a radius of about 1,230 km (760 mi), which is about 20% of Earth's radius or 70% of the Moon's radius.
The temperature at its surface is estimated to be approximately 5,700 K (5,430 °C; 9,800 °F), about the temperature at the surface of the Sun.
In 1952, Francis Birch published a detailed analysis of the available data and concluded that the inner core was probably crystalline iron.
In 2005, shear waves were detected passing through the inner core; these claims were initially controversial, but are now gaining acceptance.

narration.text: Why Earth's core matches the Sun's surface heat.
Its surface is about 5,700 kelvin.
Yet the inner core is a solid iron ball.
Crushing pressure keeps the metal from melting.

So daylight, not willpower, keeps your body on schedule.

facts.claim: It is composed of around 270 bones at birth – this total decreases to around 206 bones by adulthood after some bones fuse together.
The bone mass in the skeleton makes up about 14% of the total body weight.
Bones are a mixture of chondroitin sulfate and hydroxyapatite, the latter making up 70% of a bone.
Hydroxyapatite is in turn composed of 39.8% of calcium, 41.4% of oxygen, 18.5% of phosphorus, and 0.2% of hydrogen by mass.

narration.text: You were born with about 270 bones.
Adults have around 206.
Many bones fuse together as you grow.
Bone makes up about 14% of body weight.
About 70% of bone is a mineral called hydroxyapatite.
Keeping every baby bone would leave joints where you need solid support.
A fused skull protects the brain better than loose plates.
So growing up means having fewer bones, not more.

topics.misconception: Fusion breakeven at NIF counted laser energy on target, not the power the facility drew from the grid.
editorialTitles: What It Will Take for Fusion Power to Work
Why Fusion Breakeven Isn't Electricity Yet

facts.claim: The design uses 192 beamlines in a parallel system of flashlamp-pumped, neodymium-doped phosphate glass lasers.
The feat required a 2.05 MJ laser (up from 1.9 MJ in 2021), yielding 3.15 MJ, a 54% surplus.
On December 5, 2022, NIF reached scientific breakeven for the first time, producing 154% of the energy of the laser.
Subsequent shots have seen continued increases in yield; a February 2024 shot exceeded 5 MJ.

narration.text: Why fusion's 54% surplus isn't electricity yet.
At NIF, a 2.05 MJ laser shot yielded 3.15 MJ.
It was the first scientific breakeven, using 192 laser beams.
A 2024 shot pushed yield past 5 megajoules.
But the lasers drew far more power from the grid than that.
A power plant would need far higher gain, many times a second.
Scientific breakeven is proof of physics, not yet of electricity.
So fusion works. Making it pay is the next problem.

Why Space Elevators Wait on Chemistry

facts.claim: The greatest tension on a space elevator cable is at the point of geostationary orbit, 35,786 km (22,236 mi) above the Earth's equator.
Metals like titanium, steel or aluminium alloys have breaking lengths of only 20–30 km (0.2–0.3 MPa/(kg/m3)).
A functional Earth space elevator would require a tether of 30–80 megaYuri (corresponding to 3100–8200 km of breaking length).
In 2014, Google X found that no one had yet manufactured a perfectly formed carbon nanotube strand longer than a meter.
The design's passenger climber would be able to reach the level of geosynchronous equatorial orbit (GEO) after an 8-day trip.

narration.text: A space elevator cable must stretch past 35,786 kilometres.
No material we can make is strong enough.
Steel can hang only 20 to 30 kilometres before snapping.
An Earth elevator needs 3,100 to 8,200 kilometres of breaking length.
Carbon nanotubes could work, in theory.
But no one has made a perfect strand longer than a meter.
Even then, a climber would take about 8 days to reach orbit.
So the elevator waits on chemistry, not rocket science.

Light carries momentum, so each photon gives a tiny push.
It passed Venus at 80,800 kilometres that December.
No fuel means it can keep accelerating for years.
So sunlight can be both power and propulsion.

So first we have to learn what it's actually made of.

Neutron stars are known that have rotation periods from about 1.4 ms to 30 s.

narration.text: Why one teaspoon of neutron star would explode.
It weighs about 900 Great Pyramids.
Neutron stars pack 1.4 Suns into about 10 kilometres.
Squeeze Earth that hard, and it fits in 305 metres.
Outside the star, that matter wouldn't stay compressed.
Freed from crushing gravity, it would expand violently.
So the teaspoon isn't a weight. It's a bomb.

facts.claim: If a GRB were to occur within the Milky Way within 5,000 to 8,000 light-years and its emission were beamed straight towards Earth, the effects could be harmful and potentially devastating for its ecosystems.
GRBs deplete ozone, with models showing a possible global reduction of 25–35%, with as much as 75% in certain locations, an effect that would last for years.
The Ordovician mass extinction 450 million years ago may have been caused by a GRB.
A GRB could potentially vaporize anything in its beams' paths within a range of around 200 light-years.

narration.text: A gamma-ray burst 8,000 light-years away could devastate Earth.
It wouldn't burn us. It would strip our ozone.
Models show a global ozone loss of 25 to 35%.
In places, losses could reach 75%, lasting for years.
Unfiltered ultraviolet light would then hit plankton and crops.
One may have triggered the Ordovician extinction, 450 million years ago.
So the deadliest light in the universe works through the sky.

So visitors from other stars pass by, and we barely notice.

It remains the highest-energy cosmic ray ever observed.
It beat the top blazar photon energy 20 million times over.
That's roughly the energy of a thrown ball, in one particle.
So something in the universe accelerates particles beyond our machines.

It's the Boötes void, found in 1981.

Its center sits 700 million light-years away.
From inside, the night sky would hold almost no other galaxies.
Astronomers might not have discovered other galaxies until much later.
Galaxies gather along filaments, leaving vast gaps between.
So the universe is less a cloud than a web with holes.

It may have been half of a binary pair.
One star was captured, and its partner was launched.
It's now about 29,000 light-years from Earth.
It will never return to the Milky Way.
So black holes don't just swallow stars. They throw them.

facts.claim: He is known for having survived a radiation accident in 1978, when a high-energy proton beam from a particle accelerator passed through his head.
Bugorski was leaning over the equipment when he stuck his head in the path of the 76 GeV (12.2 nJ) proton beam.

Anatoli Bugorski was checking faulty equipment.
The safety mechanisms had failed.
The beam carried 76 GeV protons.
The dose along its path was 2,000 to 3,000 sieverts.
Because it was so narrow, most of his body was spared.
So where radiation lands matters as much as how much.

At that distance, rock itself may melt.

So the fastest spinners in the universe are also the densest.

facts.claim: GW170817 was a gravitational wave observed by the LIGO and Virgo detectors on 17 August 2017, originating within the galaxy NGC 4993, about 140 million light years away.
GW170817 had an audible duration of approximately 100 seconds and exhibited the characteristic intensity and frequency expected of the inspiral of two neutron stars.
A short gamma-ray burst of around 2 seconds was detected by the Fermi and INTEGRAL spacecraft beginning 1.7 seconds after the GW emitted by the merger.
A total of 16,000 times the mass of the Earth in heavy elements is believed to have formed, including approximately 10 Earth masses just of the two elements gold and platinum.

narration.text: One crash forged 10 Earths of gold and platinum.
LIGO heard it on 17 August 2017.
The collision was about 140 million light-years away.
Its gravitational-wave signal lasted about 100 seconds.
1.7 seconds later, a gamma-ray burst arrived.
In total, 16,000 Earth masses of heavy elements formed.
Some of the gold on Earth likely came from events like this.
So your jewellery may be debris from a stellar collision.

Magnetars are formed by the collapse of a star with a mass 10–25 times that of the Sun.
Starquakes on the surface of the magnetar often lead to extremely powerful gamma-ray flare emissions which have been recorded on Earth in 1979, 1998, and 2004.

Its field packs more mass-energy than solid metal.
Earth's field is just 30 to 60 microteslas.
A strong neodymium magnet reaches about 1.25 tesla.
Near a magnetar, atoms themselves stretch into thin rods.
Starquakes there have sent gamma-ray flares all the way to Earth.
Up close, chemistry itself would stop working.
So the strongest magnets in the universe are also the deadliest.

It barely scratched the crust.
Soviet engineers began drilling Kola SG-3 in 1970.
They aimed for 15,000 metres and fell short.
Heat stopped them: 180 °C, far above what they expected.
Rock that hot starts behaving more like plastic than stone.
Deeper down, the heat and pressure only climb.
So the planet's first defence against drilling is heat, not hardness.

Scavengers strip flesh; worms and microbes feast on bones.
Some species may live almost nowhere else.
So a single whale becomes a deep-sea ecosystem.

So without bees we'd still eat, just with far less variety.

facts.claim: The majority of Earth's atmosphere (78%) is atmospheric nitrogen, making it the largest source of nitrogen.
Between 5 and 10 billion kg per year are fixed by lightning strikes, but most fixation is done by free-living or symbiotic bacteria known as diazotrophs.
Nitrogen cannot be utilized by phytoplankton as N2 so it must undergo nitrogen fixation which is performed predominately by cyanobacteria.
High-temperature combustion has contributed to a 6- or 7-fold increase in the flux of NOx to the atmosphere.

narration.text: Air is 78% nitrogen, but plants can't use it.
Bacteria must fix it into usable forms first.
Lightning fixes 5 to 10 billion kilograms a year.
But most fixation is done by bacteria.
Ocean phytoplankton rely on cyanobacteria to fix it for them.
Combustion has raised nitrogen oxide flux 6 to 7 times.
If fixation stopped, soils and seas would slowly starve.
So the air's most common gas is useless until microbes change it.

facts.claim: The Haber process enabled the global population to increase from 1.6 billion in 1900 to 7.7 billion by November 2018.
Although atmospheric nitrogen (N2) is abundant, comprising ~78% of the air, it is exceptionally stable and does not readily react with other chemicals.
On each pass, only about 15% conversion occurs; due to the recycling of leftover reactants, eventually conversion of 97% is achieved.
The Haber process consumes 3–5% of the world's natural gas production (around 1–2% of the world's energy supply).

narration.text: Why 7.7 billion people depend on air-made fertilizer.
The Haber process pulls nitrogen from the air.
Air is about 78% nitrogen, but it barely reacts.
Each pass converts only about 15% into ammonia.
Recycling the gases eventually reaches 97% conversion.
It uses 3 to 5% of the world's natural gas.
Without it, today's harvests couldn't feed today's population.
So much of the food on your plate began as air.

facts.claim: Relativity predicted that the clocks on GPS satellites, as observed by those on Earth, run 38 microseconds faster per day than those on the Earth.
The prototype spacecraft was launched in 1978 and the full constellation of 24 satellites became operational in 1993.
When Selective Availability was discontinued, GPS was accurate to about 5 meters (16 ft).
As of March 2026, 21 GPS satellites broadcast L5 signals.

narration.text: GPS clocks gain 38 microseconds a day from relativity.
Without correction, positions would drift quickly.
The system became fully operational in 1993.
It was designed around 24 satellites.
Civil accuracy reached about 5 metres.
If it went dark, phones would lean on cell towers and Wi-Fi.
But networks and markets that use GPS timing would feel it too.
So GPS isn't just maps. It's the world's shared clock.
